Patient demographics:
  age: 18
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Project Manager
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 55

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Male Presence: Being alone with men, Transportation (Bicycle): Bicycle, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Smoking: I smoke, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

Vignette:
Kai was eighteen years old, working as a project manager for a small construction firm, a job that required him to coordinate with crews of men on job sites every day. He had been with his girlfriend for just over a year, and she was the only person he felt truly safe around. But that safety was fragile, and he knew it. What brought him to therapy was a growing sense that he was losing control of his own life—that the strategies he had developed to keep himself together were starting to unravel.

When Kai was a child, he had witnessed his father beat his mother. He could not remember the whole event. What stayed with him were pieces—the sound of a heavy hand connecting with flesh, the sharp smell of beer on his father’s breath, the sight of his mother’s body crumpling against the kitchen cabinets. The memory came in fragments that did not fit together like a normal story. There was no beginning, no middle, no end. Just terror, raw and immediate, every time a piece surfaced. And when it did, it was not like remembering something from the past. It was like being there again, his small body frozen in the doorway, his chest tight, his throat closed. The same terror he had felt at six years old would wash over him in the present moment, leaving him breathless and shaking.

In the years since, Kai had learned to manage. But his management had become a prison. He had come to believe that men were dangerous, that being alone with a man meant being vulnerable to violence. On job sites, he made sure he was never the last person in a room with a coworker. He would step out for a cigarette, or pretend he had a phone call, or simply walk away. He smoked constantly—a pack a day, sometimes more—because the ritual of lighting up gave him something to do with his hands and a reason to step outside. He drank most evenings, not to get drunk but to take the edge off the hypervigilance that hummed beneath his skin like a live wire. He had also started taking his girlfriend’s anxiety medication when she was not looking, because it helped him sleep. He knew it was not his prescription, but he told himself he needed it more than she did.

The avoidance had crept into every part of his life. He avoided people in general now—not just men. He had stopped going to the grocery store after dark. He had stopped visiting his mother because she still lived in the same house, and the smell of alcohol anywhere—even cooking wine, even hand sanitizer—sent him into a spiral. He had also stopped riding his bicycle, the one thing that had once made him feel free, because the sensation of being on two wheels, exposed and moving, reminded him of the helplessness of childhood. He could not explain why. It just did.

At home, he checked the locks on the doors and windows three or four times before bed, sometimes getting up again to check them once more. He jumped at ordinary sounds—the clatter of a dropped tool, the slam of a car door, the creak of the house settling. His girlfriend had started to notice the way he watched other people when they were out together, his eyes tracking strangers as if they were predators. He watched their hands. He watched their faces. He was certain that if he let his guard down for even a second, someone would hurt him.

What finally brought Kai to therapy was a panic attack on a job site two weeks ago. He had been alone in a storage trailer with a subcontractor, a man he had worked with for months. The man had said something ordinary—asked about a delivery—and Kai had frozen. His heart had pounded so hard he thought he might pass out. He had fled without explanation, and his boss had told him to take some time off. His girlfriend had found him crying in the bathroom when he got home. She had held him and told him he needed help. He was terrified of what would happen if he did not get better—terrified of losing his job, of losing her, of spending the rest of his life jumping at shadows. But he was also terrified of what getting better might mean: facing the pieces of a memory he had spent years trying to keep at bay.
